entries.8c33230f9c08f41f53127ffc2fff3ca4d45df00c: <div sID="gen19183" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="40" osisID="Ezek.40" sID="Ezek.40"/> <div eID="gen19183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19184" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19185" type="x-p"/> The waters of the sanctuary which this prophet saw in vision (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">ch. xlvii. 1</reference>) are a proper representation of this prophecy. Hitherto the waters have been sometimes but to the ankles, in other places to the knees, or to the loins, but now the waters have risen, and have become "a river which cannot be passed over." Here is one continued vision, beginning at this chapter, to the end of the book, which is justly looked upon to be one of the most difficult portions of scripture in all the book of God. The Jews will not allow any to read it till they are thirty years old, and tell those who do read it that, though they cannot understand every thing in it, "when Elias comes he will explain it." Many commentators, both ancient and modern, have owned themselves at a loss what to make of it and what use to make of it. But because it is hard to be understood we must not therefore throw it by, but humbly search concerning it, get as far as we can into it and as much as we can out of it, and, when we despair of satisfaction in every difficulty we meet with, bless God that our salvation does not depend upon it, but that things necessary are plain enough, and wait till God shall reveal even this unto us. These chapters are the more to be regarded because the last two chapters of the Revelation seem to have a plain allusion to them, as <reference osisRef="Rev.20.1-Rev.20.15">Rev. xx.</reference> has to the foregoing prophecy of Gog and Magog. Here is the vision of a glorious temple (in this chapter and <reference osisRef="Ezek.41.1-Ezek.42.20">ch. xli. and xlii.</reference>), of God's taking possession of it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1-Ezek.43.27">ch. xliii.</reference>), orders concerning the priests that are to minister in this temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1-Ezek.44.31">ch. xliv.</reference>), the division of the land, what portion should be allotted for the sanctuary, what for the city, and what for the prince, both in his government of the people and his worship of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.45.1-Ezek.45.25">ch. xlv.</reference>), and further instructions for him and the people, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1-Ezek.46.24">ch. xlvi.</reference> After the vision of the holy waters we have the borders of the holy land, and the portions assigned to the tribes, and the dimensions and gates of the holy city, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1-Ezek.48.35">ch. xlvii., xlviii.</reference> Some make this to represent what had been during the flourishing state of the Jewish church, how glorious Solomon's temple was in its best days, that the captives might see what they had lost by sin and might be the more humbled. But that seems not probable. The general scope of it I take to be, 1. To assure the captives that they should not only return to their own land, and be settled there, which had been often promised in the foregoing chapters, but that they should have, and therefore should be encouraged to build, another temple, which God would own, and where he would meet them and bless them, that the ordinances of worship should be revived, and the sacred priesthood should there attend; and, though they should not have a king to live in such splendour as formerly, yet they should have a prince or ruler (who is often spoken of in this vision), who should countenance the worship of God among them and should himself be an example of diligent attendance upon it, and that prince, priests, and people, should have a very comfortable settlement and subsistence in their own land. 2. To direct them to look further than all this, and to expect the coming of the Messiah, who had before been prophesied of under the name of David because he was the man that projected the building of the temple and that should set up a spiritual temple, even the gospel-church, the glory of which should far exceed that of Solomon's temple, and which should continue to the end of time. The dimensions of these visionary buildings being so large (the new temple more spacious than all the old Jerusalem and the new Jerusalem of greater extent than all the land of Canaan) plainly intimates, as Dr. Lightfoot observes, that these things cannot be literally, but must spiritually, understood. At the gospel-temple, erected by Christ and his apostles, was so closely connected with the second material temple, was erected so carefully just at the time when that fell into decay, that it might be ready to receive its glories when it resigned them, that it was proper enough that they should both be referred to in one and the same vision. Under the type and figure of a temple and altar, priests and sacrifices, is foreshown the spiritual worship that should be performed in gospel times, more agreeable to the nature both of God and man, and that perfected at last in the kingdom of glory, in which perhaps these visions will have their full accomplishment, and some think in some happy and glorious state of the gospel-church on this side heaven, in the latter days. <div eID="gen19185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19186" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A general account of this vision of the temple and city, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.1-Ezek.40.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. A particular account of it entered upon; and a description given, 1. Of the outside wall, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.5">ver. 5</reference>. 2. Of the east gate, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.6-Ezek.40.19">ver. 6-19</reference>. 3. Of the north gate, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.20-Ezek.40.23">ver. 20-23</reference>. 4. Of the south gate (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.24-Ezek.40.31">ver. 24-31</reference>) and the chambers and other appurtenances belonging to these gates. 5. Of the inner court, both towards the east and towards the south, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.39-Ezek.40.43">ver. 39-43</reference>. 7. Of the lodgings for the singers and the priests, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.44-Ezek.40.47">ver. 44-47</reference>. 8. Of the porch of the house, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.48-Ezek.40.49">ver. 48, 49</reference>.
entries.f54ba18f4e3049d662a3bf34cab4226e69b7beaf: <div eID="gen19186" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19184" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19187" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the five and twentieth year of our captivity, in the beginning of the year, in the tenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, in the fourteenth year after that the city was smitten, in the selfsame day the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was upon me, and brought me thither. <hi type="super">2</hi> In the visions of God brought he me into the land of Israel, and set me upon a very high mountain, by which <hi type="italic">was</hi> as the frame of a city on the south. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he brought me thither, and, behold, <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a man, whose appearance <hi type="italic">was</hi> like the appearance of brass, with a line of flax in his hand, and a measuring reed; and he stood in the gate. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the man said unto me, Son of man, behold with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears, and set thine heart upon all that I shall shew thee; for to the intent that I might shew <hi type="italic">them</hi> unto thee <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou brought hither: declare all that thou seest to the house of Israel. <div eID="gen19187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19188" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The date of this vision. It was in the twenty-fifth year of Ezekiel's captivity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.1">v. 1</reference>), which some compute to be the thirty-third year of the first captivity, and is here said to be the <hi type="italic">fourteenth year after the city was smitten.</hi> See how seasonably the clearest and fullest prospects of their deliverance were given, when they were in the depth of their distress, and an assurance of the return of the morning when they were in the midnight of their captivity: "Then <hi type="italic">the hand of the Lord was upon me</hi> and <hi type="italic">brought me thither</hi> to Jerusalem, now that it was in ruins, desolate and deserted"—a pitiable sight to the prophet. 2. The scene where it was laid. The prophet was brought, <hi type="italic">in the visions of God, to the land of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.2">v. 2</reference>. And it was not the first time that he had been brought thither in vision. We had him carried to Jerusalem to see it in its iniquity and shame (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">ch. viii. 3</reference>); here he is carried thither to have a pleasing prospect of it in its glory, though its present aspect, now that it was quite depopulated, was dismal. He was set <hi type="italic">upon a very high mountain,</hi> as Moses upon the top of Pisgah, to view this land, which was now a second time a <hi type="italic">land of promise,</hi> not yet in possession. From the top of this mountain he saw <hi type="italic">as the frame of a city,</hi> the plan and model of it; but this city was a temple as large as a city. The <hi type="italic">New Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.22">Rev. xxi. 22</reference>) had <hi type="italic">no temple therein;</hi> this which we have here is <hi type="italic">all temple,</hi> which comes much to one. It is a city for men to dwell in; it is a temple for God to dwell in; for in the church on earth God dwells with men, in that in heaven men dwell with God. Both these are framed in the counsel of God, framed by infinite wisdom, and all very good. 3. The particular discoveries of this city (which he had at first a general view of) were made to him by <hi type="italic">a man whose appearance was like the appearance of brass</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">v. 3</reference>), not a created angel, but Jesus Christ, who should be found in fashion as a man, that he might both discover and build the gospel-temple. He brought him to this city, for it is through Christ that we have both acquaintance with and access to the benefits and privileges of God's house. He it is that <hi type="italic">shall build the temple of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zech. vi. 13</reference>. His appearing like brass intimates both his brightness and his strength. John, in vision, saw <hi type="italic">his feet like unto fine brass,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.15">Rev. i. 15</reference>. 4. The dimensions of this city or temple, and the several parts of it, were taken with a <hi type="italic">line of flax</hi> and a <hi type="italic">measuring reed,</hi> or <hi type="italic">rod</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">v. 3</reference>), as carpenters have both their line and a wooden measure. The temple of God is built by line and rule; and those that would let others into the knowledge of it must do it by that line and rule. The church is formed according to the scripture, <hi type="italic">the pattern in the mount.</hi> That is the line and the measuring reed that is in the hand of Christ. With that doctrine and laws ought to be measured, and examined by that; for then peace is upon the Israel of God when they <hi type="italic">walk according to that rule.</hi> 5. Directions are here given to the prophet to receive this revelation from the Lord and transmit it pure and entire to the church, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.4">v. 4</reference>. (1.) He must carefully observe every thing that was said and done in this vision. His attention is raised and engaged (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold with thy eyes</hi> all that is <hi type="italic">shown thee</hi> (do not only see it, but look intently upon it), and <hi type="italic">hear with thy ears</hi> all that is <hi type="italic">said to thee;</hi> diligently hearken to it, and be sure <hi type="italic">to set thy heart upon it;</hi> attend with a fixedness of thought and a close application of mind." What we see of the works of God, and what we hear of the word of God, will do us no good unless we set out hearts upon it, as those that reckon ourselves nearly concerned in it, and expect advantage to our souls by it. (2.) He must faithfully <hi type="italic">declare it to the house of Israel,</hi> that they may have the comfort of it. Therefore he receives, that he may give. Thus the <hi type="italic">Revelation of Jesus Christ</hi> was lodged in the hands of John, that he might signify it to the churches, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Rev. i. 1</reference>. And, because he is to declare it as a message from God, he must therefore be fully apprised of it himself and much affected with it. Note, Those who are to preach God's word to others ought to study it well themselves and set their hearts upon it. Now the reason given why he must both observe it himself and declare it to the house of Israel is because to this intent he is brought hither, and has it shown to him. Note, When the things of God are shown to us it concerns us to consider to what intent they are shown to us, and, when we are sitting under the ministry of the word, to consider to what intent we are brought thither, that we may answer the end of our coming, and may not receive the grace of God, in showing us such things, in vain.
entries.5195e1e207272e43a5558de7ac4cf0df885e219c: <div eID="gen19188" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19189" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And behold a wall on the outside of the house round about, and in the man's hand a measuring reed of six cubits <hi type="italic">long</hi> by the cubit and a hand breadth: so he measured the breadth of the building, one reed; and the height, one reed. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then came he unto the gate which looketh toward the east, and went up the stairs thereof, and measured the threshold of the gate, <hi type="italic">which was</hi> one reed broad; and the other threshold <hi type="italic">of the gate, which was</hi> one reed broad. <hi type="super">7</hi> And <hi type="italic">every</hi> little chamber <hi type="italic">was</hi> one reed long, and one reed broad; and between the little chambers <hi type="italic">were</hi> five cubits; and the threshold of the gate by the porch of the gate within <hi type="italic">was</hi> one reed. <hi type="super">8</hi> He measured also the porch of the gate within, one reed. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then measured he the porch of the gate, eight cubits; and the posts thereof, two cubits; and the porch of the gate <hi type="italic">was</hi> inward. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the little chambers of the gate eastward <hi type="italic">were</hi> three on this side, and three on that side; they three <hi type="italic">were</hi> of one measure: and the posts had one measure on this side and on that side. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he measured the breadth of the entry of the gate, ten cubits; <hi type="italic">and</hi> the length of the gate, thirteen cubits. <hi type="super">12</hi> The space also before the little chambers <hi type="italic">was</hi> one cubit <hi type="italic">on this side,</hi> and the space <hi type="italic">was</hi> one cubit on that side: and the little chambers <hi type="italic">were</hi> six cubits on this side, and six cubits on that side. <hi type="super">13</hi> He measured then the gate from the roof of <hi type="italic">one</hi> little chamber to the roof of another: the breadth <hi type="italic">was</hi> five and twenty cubits, door against door. <hi type="super">14</hi> He made also posts of threescore cubits, even unto the post of the court round about the gate. <hi type="super">15</hi> And from the face of the gate of the entrance unto the face of the porch of the inner gate <hi type="italic">were</hi> fifty cubits. <hi type="super">16</hi> And <hi type="italic">there were</hi> narrow windows to the little chambers, and to their posts within the gate round about, and likewise to the arches: and windows <hi type="italic">were</hi> round about inward: and upon <hi type="italic">each</hi> post <hi type="italic">were</hi> palm trees. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then brought he me into the outward court, and, lo, <hi type="italic">there were</hi> chambers, and a pavement made for the court round about: thirty chambers <hi type="italic">were</hi> upon the pavement. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the pavement by the side of the gates over against the length of the gates <hi type="italic">was</hi> the lower pavement. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then he measured the breadth from the forefront of the lower gate unto the forefront of the inner court without, a hundred cubits eastward and northward. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the gate of the outward court that looked toward the north, he measured the length thereof, and the breadth thereof. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the little chambers thereof <hi type="italic">were</hi> three on this side and three on that side; and the posts thereof and the arches thereof were after the measure of the first gate: the length thereof <hi type="italic">was</hi> fifty cubits, and the breadth five and twenty cubits. <hi type="super">22</hi> And their windows, and their arches, and their palm trees, <hi type="italic">were</hi> after the measure of the gate that looketh toward the east; and they went up unto it by seven steps; and the arches thereof <hi type="italic">were</hi> before them. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the gate of the inner court <hi type="italic">was</hi> over against the gate toward the north, and toward the east; and he measured from gate to gate a hundred cubits. <hi type="super">24</hi> After that he brought me toward the south, and behold a gate toward the south: and he measured the posts thereof and the arches thereof according to these measures. <hi type="super">25</hi> And <hi type="italic">there were</hi> windows in it and in the arches thereof round about, like those windows: the length <hi type="italic">was</hi> fifty cubits, and the breadth five and twenty cubits. <hi type="super">26</hi> And <hi type="italic">there were</hi> seven steps to go up to it, and the arches thereof <hi type="italic">were</hi> before them: and it had palm trees, one on this side, and another on that side, upon the posts thereof. <div eID="gen19189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19190" type="x-p"/> The measuring-reed which was in the hand of the surveyor-general was mentioned before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">v. 3</reference>. Here we are told (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.5">v. 5</reference>) what was the exact length of it, which must be observed, because the house was measured by it. It was <hi type="italic">six cubits long,</hi> reckoning, not by the common cubit, but the <hi type="italic">cubit of the sanctuary,</hi> the sacred cubit, by which it was fit that this holy house should be measured, and that was a hand-breadth (that it, four inches) longer than the common cubit: the common cubit was eighteen inches, this twenty-two, see <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.13">ch. xliii. 13</reference>. Yet some of the critics contend that this <hi type="italic">measuring-reed</hi> was but six common cubits in length, and one handbreadth added to the whole. The former seems more probable. Here is an account, <div eID="gen19190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19191" type="x-p"/> I. Of the outer wall of the house, which encompassed it round, which was three yards thick and three yards high, which denotes the separation between the church and the world on every side and the divine protection which the church is under. If a wall of this vast thickness will not secure it, God himself will be <hi type="italic">a wall of fire round about it;</hi> whoever attack it will do so at their peril. <div eID="gen19191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19192" type="x-p"/> II. Of the several gates with the chambers adjoining to them. Here is no mention of the outer court of all, which was called the <hi type="italic">court of the Gentiles,</hi> some think because in gospel-times there should be such a vast confluence of Gentiles to the church that their court should be left unmeasured, to signify that the worshippers in that court should be unnumbered, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.11">11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.12">12</reference>. <div eID="gen19192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19193" type="x-p"/> 1. He begins with the <hi type="italic">east gate,</hi> because that was the usual way of entering into the lower end of the temple, the holy of holies being at the west end, in opposition to the idolatrous heathen that worshipped towards the east. Now, in the account of this gate, observe, (1.) That he went up to it by <hi type="italic">stairs</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.6">v. 6</reference>), for the gospel-church was exalted above that of the Old Testament, and when we go to worship God we must ascend; so is the call, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.1">Rev. iv. 1</reference>. Come up hither. <hi type="italic">Sursum corda—Up with your hearts.</hi> (2.) That the chambers adjoining to the gates were but <hi type="italic">little chambers,</hi> about ten feet square, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.7">v. 7</reference>. These were for those to lodge in who attended the service of the house. And it becomes such as are made spiritual priests to God to content themselves with little chambers and not to seek great things to themselves; so that we may but have a place within the verge of God's court we have reason to be thankful though it be in a little chamber, a mean apartment, though we be but door-keepers there. (3.) The chambers, as they were each of them four-square, denoting their stability and due proportion and their exact agreement with the rule (for they were each of them one reed long and one reed broad), so they were all of <hi type="italic">one measure,</hi> that there might be an equality among the attendants on the service of the house. (4.) The chambers were very many; for in our Father's house there are <hi type="italic">many mansions</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.14.2">John xiv. 2</reference>), in his house above, and in that here on earth. In the secret of his tabernacle shall those be hid, and in a safe pavilion, whose desire is to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of their life, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4-Ps.27.5">Ps. xxvii. 4, 5</reference>. Some make these chambers to represent the particular congregations of believers, which are parts of the great temple, the universal church, which are, and must be, framed by the scripture-line and rule, and which Jesus Christ takes the measure of, that is, takes cognizance of, for he walks in the midst of the seven golden candle-sticks. (5.) It is said (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">He made also the posts.</hi> He that now measured them was the same that made them; for Christ is the builder of his church and therefore is best able to give us the knowledge of it. And his reducing them to the rule and standard is called his making them, for no account is made of them further than they agree with that. <hi type="italic">To the law and to the testimony.</hi> (6.) Here are posts of sixty cubits, which, some think, was literally fulfilled when Cyrus, in his edict for rebuilding the temple at Jerusalem, ordered that the height thereof should be sixty cubits, that is, thirty yards and more, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.3">Ezra vi. 3</reference>. (7.) Here were windows to the little chambers, and windows to <hi type="italic">the posts and arches</hi> (that is, to the cloisters below), and <hi type="italic">windows round about</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.16">v. 16</reference>), to signify the light from heaven with which the church is illuminated; divine revelation is let into it for instruction, direction, and comfort, to those that dwell in God's house, light to work by, light to walk by, light to see themselves and one another by. There were lights to the little chambers; even the least, and least considerable, parts and members of the church, shall have light afforded them. <hi type="italic">All thy children shall be taught of the Lord.</hi> But they are <hi type="italic">narrow windows,</hi> as those in the temple, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.4">1 Kings vi. 4</reference>. The discoveries made to the church on earth are but narrow and scanty compared with what shall be in the future state, when we shall no longer <hi type="italic">see through a glass darkly.</hi> (8.) Divers courts are here spoken of, an outermost of all, then an outer court, then an inner, and then the innermost of all, into which the priests only entered, which (some think) may put us in mind "of the diversities of gifts, and graces, and offices, in the several members of Christ's mystical body here, as also of the several degrees of glory in the courts and mansions of heaven, as there are stars in several spheres and stars of several magnitudes in the fixed firmament." <hi type="italic">English Annotations.</hi> Some draw nearer to God than others and have a more intimate acquaintance with divine things; but to a child of God a day in any of his courts is <hi type="italic">better than a thousand</hi> elsewhere. These courts had porches, or piazzas, round them, for the shelter of those that attended in them from wind and weather; for when we are in the way of our duty to God we may believe ourselves to be under his special protection, that he will graciously provide for us, nay, that he will himself be to us <hi type="italic">a covert from the storm and tempest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5-Isa.4.6">Isa. iv. 5, 6</reference>. (9.) On the posts were palm-trees engraven (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.16">v. 16</reference>), to signify that <hi type="italic">the righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree</hi> in the courts of God's house, <reference osisRef="Ps.92.12">Ps. xcii. 12</reference>. The more they are depressed with the burden of affliction the more strongly do they grow, as they say of the palm-trees. It likewise intimates the saints' victory and triumph over their spiritual enemies; they have <hi type="italic">palms in their hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>); but lest they should drop these, or have them snatched out of their hands, they are here engraven upon the posts of the temple as perpetual monuments of their honour. <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God, who always causes us to triumph.</hi> Nay, believers shall themselves be made pillars in the temple of our God, and shall <hi type="italic">go no more out,</hi> and shall have his name engraven on them, which will be their brightest ornament and honour, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Rev. iii. 12</reference>. (10.) Notice is here taken of the pavement of the court, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.17-Ezek.40.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. The word intimates that the pavement was made of <hi type="italic">porphyry—stone,</hi> which was of the colour of <hi type="italic">burning coals;</hi> for the brightest and most sparkling glories of this world should be put and kept under our feet when we draw near to God and are attending upon him. The stars are, as it were, the <hi type="italic">burning coals,</hi> or stones of a <hi type="italic">fiery colour,</hi> with which the pavement of God's celestial temple is laid; and, if the pavement of the court be so bright and glittering, how glorious must we conclude the mansions of that house to be! <div eID="gen19193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19194" type="x-p"/> 2. The gates that looked towards the north (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.20">v. 20</reference>) and towards the south (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.24">v. 24</reference>), with their appurtenances, are much the same with that towards the east, <hi type="italic">after the measure of the first gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.21">v. 21</reference>. But the description is repeated very particularly. And thus largely was the structure of the tabernacle related in Exodus, and of the temple in the books of Kings and Chronicles, to signify the special notice God does take, and his ministers should take, of all that belong to his church. His delight is in them; his eye is upon them. He knows all that are his, all his living temples and all that belongs to them. Observe, (1.) This temple had not only a gate towards the east, to let into it the <hi type="italic">children of the east,</hi> that were famous for their wealth and wisdom, but it had a gate to the north, and another to the south, for the admission of the poorer and less civilized nations. The new Jerusalem has <hi type="italic">twelve gates,</hi> three towards each quarter of the world (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.13">Rev. xxi. 13</reference>); for many shall come from all parts to sit down there, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.11">Matt. viii. 11</reference>. (2.) To those gates they went up by steps, <hi type="italic">seven steps</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.22-Ezek.40.26">v. 22-26</reference>), which, as some observe, may remind us of the necessity of advancing in grace and holiness, adding one grace to another, going from step to step, <hi type="italic">from strength to strength,</hi> still pressing forward towards perfection—upward, upward, towards heaven, the temple above.
entries.5316d9e6b40aa8e357d5f5f70dad25032a9d943d: <div eID="gen19194" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19195" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> And <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a gate in the inner court toward the south: and he measured from gate to gate toward the south a hundred cubits. <hi type="super">28</hi> And he brought me to the inner court by the south gate: and he measured the south gate according to these measures; <hi type="super">29</hi> And the little chambers thereof, and the posts thereof, and the arches thereof, according to these measures: and <hi type="italic">there were</hi> windows in it and in the arches thereof round about: <hi type="italic">it was</hi> fifty cubits long, and five and twenty cubits broad. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the arches round about <hi type="italic">were</hi> five and twenty cubits long, and five cubits broad. <hi type="super">31</hi> And the arches thereof <hi type="italic">were</hi> toward the utter court; and palm trees <hi type="italic">were</hi> upon the posts thereof: and the going up to it <hi type="italic">had</hi> eight steps. <hi type="super">32</hi> And he brought me into the inner court toward the east: and he measured the gate according to these measures. <hi type="super">33</hi> And the little chambers thereof, and the posts thereof, and the arches thereof, <hi type="italic">were</hi> according to these measures: and <hi type="italic">there were</hi> windows therein and in the arches thereof round about: <hi type="italic">it was</hi> fifty cubits long, and five and twenty cubits broad. <hi type="super">34</hi> And the arches thereof <hi type="italic">were</hi> toward the outward court; and palm trees <hi type="italic">were</hi> upon the posts thereof, on this side, and on that side: and the going up to it <hi type="italic">had</hi> eight steps. <hi type="super">35</hi> And he brought me to the north gate, and measured <hi type="italic">it</hi> according to these measures; <hi type="super">36</hi> The little chambers thereof, the posts thereof, and the arches thereof, and the windows to it round about: the length <hi type="italic">was</hi> fifty cubits, and the breadth five and twenty cubits. <hi type="super">37</hi> And the posts thereof <hi type="italic">were</hi> toward the utter court; and palm trees <hi type="italic">were</hi> upon the posts thereof, on this side, and on that side: and the going up to it <hi type="italic">had</hi> eight steps. <hi type="super">38</hi> And the chambers and the entries thereof <hi type="italic">were</hi> by the posts of the gates, where they washed the burnt offering. <div eID="gen19195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19196" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have a delineation of the inner court. The survey of the outer court ended with the south side of it. This of the inner court begins with the south side (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.27">v. 27</reference>), proceeds to the east (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.32">v. 32</reference>), and so to the north (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.35">v. 35</reference>); for here is no gate either of the outer or inner court towards the <hi type="italic">west.</hi> It should seem that in Solomon's temple there were gates westward, for we find porters towards the west, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.24">1 Chron. ix. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.8">xxvi. 8</reference>. But Josephus says that in the second temple there was no gate on the west side. Observe, 1. These gates into the inner court were exactly uniform with those into the outer court, the dimensions the same, the chambers adjoining the same, the galleries or rows round the court the same, and the very engravings on the posts the same. The work of grace, and its workings, are the same, for substance, in grown Christians that they are in young beginners, only that the former have got so much nearer their perfection. The faith of all the saints is alike precious, though it be not alike strong. There is a great resemblance between one child of God and another; for <hi type="italic">all they are brethren</hi> and bear the same image. 2. The ascent into the outer court at each gate was by <hi type="italic">seven steps,</hi> but the ascent into the inner court at each gate was by <hi type="italic">eight steps.</hi> This is expressly taken notice of (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.31">v. 31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.34">34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.37">37</reference>), to signify that the nearer we approach to God the more we should rise above this world and the things of it. The people, who worshipped in the outer court, must rise seven steps above other people, but the priests, who attended in the inner court, must rise eight steps above them, must exceed them at least one step more than they exceed other people.
entries.8e4dc4022a461224d7ed7153087798792d0e1755: <div eID="gen19196" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19197" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">39</hi> And in the porch of the gate <hi type="italic">were</hi> two tables on this side, and two tables on that side, to slay thereon the burnt offering and the sin offering and the trespass offering. <hi type="super">40</hi> And at the side without, as one goeth up to the entry of the north gate, <hi type="italic">were</hi> two tables; and on the other side, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> at the porch of the gate, <hi type="italic">were</hi> two tables. <hi type="super">41</hi> Four tables <hi type="italic">were</hi> on this side, and four tables on that side, by the side of the gate; eight tables, whereupon they slew <hi type="italic">their sacrifices.</hi> <hi type="super">42</hi> And the four tables <hi type="italic">were</hi> of hewn stone for the burnt offering, of a cubit and a half long, and a cubit and a half broad, and one cubit high: whereupon also they laid the instruments wherewith they slew the burnt offering and the sacrifice. <hi type="super">43</hi> And within <hi type="italic">were</hi> hooks, a hand broad, fastened round about: and upon the tables <hi type="italic">was</hi> the flesh of the offering. <hi type="super">44</hi> And without the inner gate <hi type="italic">were</hi> the chambers of the singers in the inner court, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> at the side of the north gate; and their prospect <hi type="italic">was</hi> toward the south: one at the side of the east gate <hi type="italic">having</hi> the prospect toward the north. <hi type="super">45</hi> And he said unto me, This chamber, whose prospect <hi type="italic">is</hi> toward the south, <hi type="italic">is</hi> for the priests, the keepers of the charge of the house. <hi type="super">46</hi> And the chamber whose prospect <hi type="italic">is</hi> toward the north <hi type="italic">is</hi> for the priests, the keepers of the charge of the altar: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Zadok among the sons of Levi, which come near to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to minister unto him. <hi type="super">47</hi> So he measured the court, a hundred cubits long, and an hundred cubits broad, four-square; and the altar <hi type="italic">that was</hi> before the house. <hi type="super">48</hi> And he brought me to the porch of the house, and measured <hi type="italic">each</hi> post of the porch, five cubits on this side, and five cubits on that side: and the breadth of the gate <hi type="italic">was</hi> three cubits on this side, and three cubits on that side. <hi type="super">49</hi> The length of the porch <hi type="italic">was</hi> twenty cubits, and the breadth eleven cubits; and <hi type="italic">he brought me</hi> by the steps whereby they went up to it: and <hi type="italic">there were</hi> pillars by the posts, one on this side, and another on that side. <div eID="gen19197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19198" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have an account, <div eID="gen19198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19199" type="x-p"/> I. Of the tables that were in the porch of the gates of the inner court. We find no description of the altars of burnt-offerings in the midst of that court till <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.13">ch. xliii. 13</reference>. But, because the one altar under the law was to be exchanged for a multitude of tables under the gospel, here is <hi type="italic">early notice</hi> taken of the tables, at our entrance into the inner court; for till we come to partake of the <hi type="italic">table of the Lord</hi> we are but professors at large; our admission to that is our entrance into the inner court. But in this gospel-temple we meet with no altar till after the glory of the Lord has taken possession of it, for Christ is our altar, that sanctifies every gift. Here were eight tables provided, whereon to <hi type="italic">slay the sacrifices,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.41">v. 41</reference>. We read not of any tables for this purpose either in the tabernacle or in Solomon's temple. But here they are provided, to intimate the multitude of spiritual sacrifices that should be brought to God's house in gospel-times, and the multitude of hands that should be employed in offering up those sacrifices. Here were the shambles for the altar; here were the dressers on which they laid the flesh of the sacrifice, the knives with which they cut it up, and the hooks on which they hung it up, that it might be ready to be offered on the altar (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.43">v. 43</reference>), and there also they washed the burnt-offerings (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.38">v. 38</reference>), to intimate that before we draw near to God's altar we must have every thing in readiness, must wash our hands, our hearts, those spiritual sacrifices, and so <hi type="italic">compass God's altar.</hi> <div eID="gen19199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19200" type="x-p"/> II. The use that some of the chambers mentioned before were put to. 1. Some were for the <hi type="italic">singers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.44">v. 44</reference>. It should seem they were first provided for before any other that attended this temple-service, to intimate, not only that the singing of psalms should still continue a gospel-ordinance, but that the gospel should furnish all that embrace it with abundant matter for joy and praise, and give them occasion to <hi type="italic">break forth into singing,</hi> which is often foretold concerning gospel times, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Ps. xcvi. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">xcviii. 1</reference>. Christians should be singers. <hi type="italic">Blessed are those that dwell in God's house,</hi> they will be <hi type="italic">still praising him.</hi> 2. Others of them were for <hi type="italic">the priests,</hi> both those that kept <hi type="italic">the charge of the house,</hi> to cleanse it, and to see that none came into it to pollute it, and to keep it in good repair (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.45">v. 45</reference>), and those that <hi type="italic">kept the charge of the altar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.46">v. 46</reference>), that <hi type="italic">came near to the Lord to minister to him.</hi> God will find convenient lodging for all his servants. Those that do the work of his house shall enjoy the comforts of it. <div eID="gen19200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19201" type="x-p"/> III. Of the inner court, the court of the priests, which was fifty yards square, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.47">v. 47</reference>. The altar that <hi type="italic">was before the house</hi> was placed in the midst of this court, over-against the three gates, and, standing in a direct line with the three gates of the outer court, when the gates were set open all the people in the outer court might through them be spectators of the service done at the altar. Christ is both our altar and our sacrifice, to whom we must look with an eye of faith in all our approaches to God, and he is salvation in the midst of the earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.12">Ps. lxxiv. 12</reference>), to be looked unto from all quarters. <div eID="gen19201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19202" type="x-p"/> IV. Of the porch of the house. The temple is called the house, emphatically, as if no other house were worthy to be called so. Before this house there was a porch, to teach us not to rush hastily and inconsiderately into the presence of God, but gradually, that is, gravely, and with solemnity, passing first through the outer court, then the inner, then the porch, ere we enter into the house. Between this porch and the altar was a place where the priests used to pray, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.17">Joel ii. 17</reference>. In the porch, besides the posts on which the doors were hung, there were pillars, probably for state and ornament, like <hi type="italic">Jachin</hi> and <hi type="italic">Boaz—He will establish; in him is strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.49">v. 49</reference>. In the gospel church every thing is strong and firm, and every thing ought to be kept in its place and to be done decently and in order.  <chapter eID="Ezek.40"/> <div eID="gen19202" type="x-p"/>

entries.fb0edfc6773fac046dfc9ce882c12709dd3ea37d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11808"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 40</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.40.1-Ezek.40.49">Eze 40:1-49</reference>. The Remaining Chapters, the Fortieth through Forty-eighth, Give an Ideal Picture of the Restored Jewish Temple.</title> <div sID="gen21370" type="x-p"/> The arrangements as to the land and the temple are, in many particulars, different from those subsisting before the captivity. There are things in it so improbable physically as to preclude a purely literal interpretation. The general truth seems to hold good that, as Israel served the nations for his rejection of Messiah, so shall they serve him in the person of Messiah, when he shall acknowledge Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.12">Is 60:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.17-Zech.14.19">Zec 14:17-19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.72.11">Psa 72:11</reference>). The ideal temple exhibits, under Old Testament forms (used as being those then familiar to the men whom Ezekiel, a priest himself, and one who delighted in sacrificial images, addresses), not the precise literal outline, but the essential character of the worship of Messiah as it shall be when He shall exercise sway in Jerusalem among His own people, the Jews, and thence to the ends of the earth. The very fact that the whole is a vision (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.2">Eze 40:2</reference>), not an oral face-to-face communication such as that granted to Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.12.6-Num.12.8">Nu 12:6-8</reference>), implies that the directions are not to be understood so precisely literally as those given to the Jewish lawgiver. The description involves things which, taken literally, almost involve natural impossibilities. The square of the temple, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.20">Eze 42:20</reference>, is six times as large as the circuit of the wall enclosing the old temple, and larger than all the earthly Jerusalem. Ezekiel gives three and a half miles and one hundred forty yards to his temple square. The boundaries of the ancient city were about two and a half miles. Again, the city in Ezekiel has an area between three or four thousand square miles, including the holy ground set apart for the prince, priests, and Levites. This is nearly as large as the whole of Judea west of the Jordan. As Zion lay in the center of the ideal city, the one-half of the sacred portion extended to nearly thirty miles south of Jerusalem, that is, covered nearly the whole southern territory, which reached only to the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.19">Eze 47:19</reference>), and yet five tribes were to have their inheritance on that side of Jerusalem, beyond the sacred portion (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.23-Ezek.48.28">Eze 48:23-28</reference>). Where was land to be found for them there? A breadth of but four or five miles apiece would be left. As the boundaries of the land are given the same as under Moses, these incongruities cannot be explained away by supposing physical changes about to be effected in the land such as will meet the difficulties of the purely literal interpretation. The distribution of the land is in equal portions among the twelve tribes, without respect to their relative numbers, and the parallel sections running from east to west. There is a difficulty also in the supposed separate existence of the twelve tribes, such separate tribeships no longer existing, and it being hard to imagine how they could be restored as distinct tribes, mingled as they now are. So the stream that issued from the east threshold of the temple and flowed into the Dead Sea, in the rapidity of its increase and the quality of its waters, is unlike anything ever known in Judea or elsewhere in the world. Lastly, the catholicity of the Christian dispensation, and the spirituality of its worship, seem incompatible with a return to the local narrowness and "beggarly elements" of the Jewish ritual and carnal ordinances, disannulled "because of the unprofitableness thereof" [Fairbairn], (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.3">Ga 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">He 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.18">10:18</reference>). "A temple with sacrifices now would be a denial of the all-sufficiency of the sacrifice of Christ. He who sacrificed before confessed the Messiah. He who should sacrifice now would solemnly deny Him" [Douglas]. These difficulties, however, may be all seeming, not real. Faith accepts God's Word as it is, waits for the event, sure that it will clear up all such difficulties. Perhaps, as some think, the beau ideal of a sacred commonwealth is given according to the then existing pattern of temple services, which would be the imagery most familiar to the prophet and his hearers at the time. The minute particularizing of details is in accordance with Ezekiel's style, even in describing purely ideal scenes. The old temple embodied in visible forms and rites spiritual truths affecting the people even when absent from it. So this ideal temple is made in the absence of the outward temple to serve by description the same purpose of symbolical instruction as the old literal temple did by forms and acts. As in the beginning God promised to be a "sanctuary" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.16">Eze 11:16</reference>) to the captives at the Chebar, so now at the close is promised a complete restoration and realization of the theocratic worship and polity under Messiah in its noblest ideal (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.31.38-Jer.31.40">Jr 31:38-40</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rev.21.22">Re 21:22</reference> "no temple" is seen, as in the perfection of the new dispensation the accidents of place and form are no longer needed to realize to Christians what Ezekiel imparts to Jewish minds by the imagery familiar to them. In Ezekiel's temple holiness stretches over the entire temple, so that in this there is no longer a distinction between the different parts, as in the old temple: parts left undeterminate in the latter obtain now a divine sanction, so that all arbitrariness is excluded. So that it is be a perfect manifestation of the love of God to His covenant-people (Eze 40:1-43:12); and from it, as from a new center of religious life, there gushes forth the fulness of blessings to them, and so to all people (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.23">Eze 47:1-23</reference>) [Fairbairn and Havernick]. The temple built at the return from Babylon can only very partially have realized the model here given. The law is seemingly opposed to the gospel (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.21">Mt 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.27">22, 27</reference>, 28, 33, 34). It is not really so (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.5.17">Mt 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.31">Ro 3:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.21">Ga 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.22">22</reference>). It is true Christ's sacrifice superseded the law sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.12-Heb.10.18">He 10:12-18</reference>). Israel's province may hereafter be to show the essential identity, even in the minute details of the temple sacrifices, between the law and gospel (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.8">Ro 10:8</reference>). The ideal of the theocratic temple will then first be realized.<div eID="gen21370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11808"/><hi type="bold">1. beginning of the year--</hi>the ecclesiastical year, the first month of which was Nisan.<div eID="gen21371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the city ... thither--</hi>Jerusalem, the center to which all the prophet's thoughts tended. <div eID="gen21372" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdb14de997a58db1e85824b5c2df49750c931c9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11809"/><div sID="gen21373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11809"/><hi type="bold">2. visions of God--</hi>divinely sent visions.<div eID="gen21373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">very high mountain--</hi>Moriah, very high, as compared with the plains of Babylon, still more so as to its moral elevation (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22">Eze 17:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.40">20:40</reference>).<div eID="gen21374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by which--</hi>Ezekiel coming from the north is set down at (as the Hebrew for "upon" may be translated) Mount Moriah, and sees the city-like frame of the temple stretching southward. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">Eze 40:3</reference>, "God brings him thither," that is, close up to it, so as to inspect it minutely (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.10">Re 21:10</reference>). In this closing vision, as in the opening one of the book, the divine hand is laid on the prophet, and he is borne away in the visions of God. But the scene there was by the Chebar, Jehovah having forsaken Jerusalem; now it is the mountain of God, Jehovah having returned thither; there, the vision was calculated to inspire terror; here, hope and assurance. <div eID="gen21375" type="x-p"/>
entries.6af2fb0eb5f70343eb2beb37b708b2da30f8df61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11810"/><div sID="gen21376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11810"/><hi type="bold">3. man--</hi>The Old Testament manifestations of heavenly beings as men prepared men's minds for the coming incarnation.<div eID="gen21376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brass--</hi>resplendent.<div eID="gen21377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">line--</hi>used for longer measurements (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.1">Zec 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen21378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reed--</hi>used in measuring houses (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.15">Re 21:15</reference>). It marked the straightness of the walls. <div eID="gen21379" type="x-p"/>
entries.e85b32a438622673dfc35bbf13b30925c0c30d83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11811"/><div sID="gen21380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11811"/>5. Measures were mostly taken from the human body. The greater cubit, the length from the elbow to the end of the middle finger, a little more than two feet: exceeding the ordinary cubit (from the elbow to the wrist) by an hand-breadth, that is, twenty-one inches in all. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.13">Eze 43:13</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.5">Eze 40:5</reference>. The palm was the full breadth of the hand, three and a half inches.<div eID="gen21380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breadth of the building--</hi>that is, the boundary wall. The imperfections in the old temple's boundary wall were to have no place here. The buildings attached to it had been sometimes turned to common uses; for example, Jeremiah was imprisoned in one (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.2">Jr 20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.26">29:26</reference>). But now all these were to be holy to the Lord. The gates and doorways to the city of God were to be imprinted in their architecture with the idea of the exclusion of everything defiled (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">Re 21:27</reference>). The east gate was to be especially sacred, as it was through it the glory of God had departed (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">Eze 11:23</reference>), and through it the glory was to return (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1">Eze 43:1</reference>, 2; 44:2, 3). <div eID="gen21381" type="x-p"/>
entries.59d1b4836ca86d19461c341365b2b1781d3f2302: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11812"/><div sID="gen21382" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11812"/><hi type="bold">6. the stairs--</hi>seven in number (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.26">Eze 40:26</reference>).<div eID="gen21382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">threshold--</hi>the sill [Fairbairn].<div eID="gen21383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">other threshold--</hi>Fairbairn considers there is but one threshold, and translates, "even the one threshold, one rod broad." But there is another threshold mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.7">Eze 40:7</reference>. The two thresholds here seem to be the upper and the lower. <div eID="gen21384" type="x-p"/>
entries.4705dd0ec5f0144da83d0dc00c6f1a4784d83f3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11813"/><div sID="gen21385" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11813"/><hi type="bold">7. chamber--</hi>These chambers were for the use of the Levites who watched at the temple gates; guard-chambers (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.4">2Ki 22:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.26">1Ch 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.27">27</reference>); also used for storing utensils and musical instruments. <div eID="gen21385" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b0d4615daed2200f75cfe57f585c688ce72d37e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11814"/><div sID="gen21386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11814"/><hi type="bold">9. posts--</hi>projecting column-faced fronts of the sides of the doorway, opposite to one another. <div eID="gen21386" type="x-p"/>
entries.4277c53ccf5a91ca9ee076a40a374562df981dbf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11815"/><div sID="gen21387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11815"/><hi type="bold">12. space--</hi>rather, "the boundary." <div eID="gen21387" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f14832bf60e4016cfb3553065dae4281fb13bb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11816"/><div sID="gen21388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11816"/><hi type="bold">16. narrow--</hi>latticed [Henderson]. The ancients had no glass, so they had them latticed, narrow in the interior of the walls, and widening at the exterior. "Made fast," or "firmly fixed in the chambers" [Maurer].<div eID="gen21388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">arches--</hi>rather, "porches." <div eID="gen21389" type="x-p"/>
entries.847506605525a1b1beab9d833d1d64b50433bde6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11817"/><div sID="gen21390" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11817"/><hi type="bold">17. pavement--</hi>tesselated mosaic (<reference osisRef="Esth.1.6">Es 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen21390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chambers--</hi>serving as lodgings for the priests on duty in the temple, and as receptacles of the tithes of salt, wine, and oil. <div eID="gen21391" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a4a023ba59eaf6ea9c200232a427c726d26d39f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11818"/><div sID="gen21392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11818"/>18. The higher pavement was level with the entrance of the gates, the lower was on either side of the raised pavement thus formed. Whereas Solomon's temple had an outer court open to alterations and even idolatrous innovations (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2Ki 23:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.5">1Ch 20:5</reference>), in this there was to be no room for human corruptions. Its compass was exactly defined, one hundred cubits; and the fine pavement implied it was to be trodden only by clean feet (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Is 35:8</reference>). <div eID="gen21392" type="x-p"/>
entries.60de84c7dacd0535d3d9c99a45cce585ea64f95f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11819"/><div sID="gen21393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11819"/>20-27. The different approaches corresponded in plan. In the case of these two other gates, however, no mention is made of a building with thirty chambers such as was found on the east side. Only one was needed, and it was assigned to the east as being the sacred quarter, and that most conveniently situated for the officiating priests. <div eID="gen21393" type="x-p"/>
entries.af7f5eb9117d05c9a0d17e42383dc856f1e0c4f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11821"/><div sID="gen21395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11821"/>28-37. The inner court and its gates.<div eID="gen21395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to these measures--</hi>namely, the measures of the outer gate. The figure and proportions of the inner answered to the outer. <div eID="gen21396" type="x-p"/>
entries.81a9a1a65c2b06e06e170e70a5122092a521e56e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11825"/><div sID="gen21401" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11825"/><hi type="bold">38. chambers ... entries--</hi>literally, "a chamber and its door."<div eID="gen21401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the posts--</hi>that is, at or close by the posts or columns.<div eID="gen21402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">where they washed the burnt offering--</hi>This does not apply to all the gates but only to the north gate. For <reference osisRef="Lev.1.11">Le 1:11</reference> directs the sacrifices to be killed north of the altar; and <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5">Eze 8:5</reference> calls the north gate, "the gate of the altar." And <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.40">Eze 40:40</reference> particularly mentions the north gate. <div eID="gen21403" type="x-p"/>
entries.74fd04916d70c9cce48c958bf9868279e00b3a1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11826"/><div sID="gen21404" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11826"/><hi type="bold">43. hooks--</hi>cooking apparatus for cooking the flesh of the sacrifices that fell to the priests. The hooks were "fastened" in the walls within the apartment, to hang the meat from, so as to roast it. The Hebrew comes from a root "fixed" or "placed." <div eID="gen21404" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3ba266cd259df519f72c621d96bcf161a7b1f3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11827"/><div sID="gen21405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11827"/><hi type="bold">44. the chambers of the singers--</hi>two in number, as proved by what follows: "and their prospect (that is, the prospect of one) was toward the south, (and) one toward the north." So the Septuagint. <div eID="gen21405" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b3248bb25af789c108d03aaf1d9bbd93ffb98cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11828"/><div sID="gen21406" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11828"/><hi type="bold">46. Zadok--</hi>lineally descended from Aaron. He had the high priesthood conferred on him by Solomon, who had set aside the family of Ithamar because of the part which Abiathar had taken in the rebellion of Adonijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.7">1Ki 1:7</reference>; 2:26, 27). <div eID="gen21406" type="x-p"/>
entries.fdcc37b274bfa522eef430fa5eafd8a62d6f86b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11829"/><div sID="gen21407" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11829"/><hi type="bold">47. court, an hundred cubits ... foursquare--</hi>not to be confounded with the inner court, or court of Israel, which was open to all who had sacrifices to bring, and went round the three sides of the sacred territory, one hundred cubits broad. This court was one hundred cubits square, and had the altar in it, in front of the temple. It was the court of the priests, and hence is connected with those who had charge of the altar and the music. The description here is brief, as the things connected with this portion were from the first divinely regulated. <div eID="gen21407" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a46e1529cff7ba6a50a347bae7edaf87b94b347: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11830"/><div sID="gen21408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11830"/>48-49. These two verses belong to the forty-first chapter, which treats of the temple itself. <div eID="gen21408" type="x-p"/>

entries.552722947641a9f608fefbf2d4fdf8c320e6895c: <div eID="gen32470" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32471" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32472" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32472" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32471" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32473" type="x-p"/> The prophecy or vision, which begins here, continues to the end of the Book. The Temple of Jerusalem lying in ruins when Ezekiel had this vision, (for its date as the fourteenth year after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar), the Jews needed consolation. If they were not promised a restoration of the temple, they would not feel so great an interest in returning home. It is thought by some that no model of Solomon's Temple had remained. To direct them, therefore, in the dimensions, parts, order, and rules of their new temple might be one reason why Ezekiel is so particular in the description of the old; to which the new was conformable in figure and parts, though inferior in magnificence, on account of the poverty of the nation at the time. Whatever was august or illustrious in the prophetic figures, and not literally fulfilled in or near their own times, the ancient Jews properly considered as belonging to the time of the Messiah. Accordingly, upon finding that the latter temple fell short of the model of the temple here described by Ezekiel, they supposed the prophecy to refer, at least in part, to the period now mentioned. And we, who live under the Gospel dispensation, have apostolical authority for the assertion that the temple and temple worship were emblematic of Christ's Church, frequently represented in the New Testament under the metaphor of a temple, in allusion to the symmetry, beauty, and firmness of that of Solomon; to its orderly worship; and to the manifestations it held of the Divine Presence. This chapter commences with the time, manner, and end of the vision, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.1-Eze.40.5">Eze 40:1-5</reference>. We have next a description of the east gate, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.6-Eze.40.19">Eze 40:6-19</reference>, the north gate, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.20-Eze.40.22">Eze 40:20-22</reference>, and the south gate, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.24-Eze.40.31">Eze 40:24-31</reference>. A farther description of the east gate, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.32-Eze.40.34">Eze 40:32-34</reference>, and of the north gate, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.35-Eze.40.38">Eze 40:35-38</reference>. Account of the eight tables, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.39-Eze.40.43">Eze 40:39-43</reference>; of the chambers, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.44-Eze.40.47">Eze 40:44-47</reference>; and of the porch of the temple, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.48">Eze 40:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.49">Eze 40:49</reference>. <div eID="gen32473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32474" type="x-p"/> A New Plan of the Temple at Jerusalem <div eID="gen32474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32475" type="x-p"/> For an explanation of this plan, and of the accompanying map of the division of the Land of Canaan, see the notes at end of Ezekiel 48. <div eID="gen32475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32476" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32477" type="x-p"/> In the five and twentieth year of our captivity - According to the date here given, this prophecy was delivered on Tuesday, April 20, A.M. 3430, in the twenty-fifth year of the captivity of Jeconiah, and fourteen years after the taking of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen32477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32478" type="x-p"/> The temple here described by Ezekiel is, in all probability, the same which he saw before his captivity, and which had been burned by the Chaldeans fourteen years before this vision. On comparing the Books of Kings and Chronicles with this prophet, we shall find the same dimensions in the parts described by both; for instance, the temple, or place which comprehended the sanctuary, the holy place, and the vestibule or porch before the temple, is found to measure equally the same both in Ezekiel and the Kings. Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.3-1Kgs.6.16">1Kgs 6:3-16</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Eze.41.2">Eze 41:2</reference>, etc. The inside ornaments of the temple are entirely the same; in both we see two courts; an inner one for the priests, and an outer one for the people. Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.29-1Kgs.6.36">1Kgs 6:29-36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.4.9">2Chr 4:9</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Eze.41.16">Eze 41:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.41.17">Eze 41:17</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eze.48.7-Eze.48.10">Eze 48:7-10</reference>. So that there is room to suppose that, in all the rest, the temple of Ezekiel resembled the old one; and that God's design in retracing these ideas in the prophet's memory was to preserve the remembrance of the plan, the dimensions, the ornaments, and whole structure of this Divine edifice; and that at the return from captivity the people might more easily repair it, agreeably to this model. The prophet's applying himself to describe this edifice was a motive of hope to the Jews of seeing themselves one day delivered from captivity, the temple rebuilt, and their nation restored to its ancient inheritance. Ezekiel touches very slightly upon the description of the temple or house of the Lord, which comprehended the holy place or sanctuary, and which are so exactly described in the Books of Kings. He dwells more largely upon the gates, the galleries, and apartments, of the temple, concerning which the history of the kings had not spoken, or only just taken notice of by the way. <div eID="gen32478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32479" type="x-p"/> This is the judgment of Calmet; and although every Biblical critic is of the same opinion, yet more labor is spent on rebuilding this temple of Ezekiel than was spent on that built by Solomon! The Jesuits, Prada and Villalpand, have given three folio volumes on this temple, with abundance of cuts, where the different parts are exhibited after the finest models of Grecian and Roman architecture! But still the building is incomplete. Now, of what consequence is all this to the Christian, or to any other reader? I confess I see not. While, then, we have the exact dimensions and accurate description in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, of that built by Solomon, in imitation of which this plan by Ezekiel was drawn, we need not be very solicitous about the manner of measuring and describing used by the prophet; as, when we have labored through the whole, we have only the measurements and description of that built by Solomon, and delineated by a hand not less faithful in the First Book of Kings, <reference osisRef="Eze.6.1-Eze.6.14">Eze 6:1-14</reference>, and 2 Chronicles 2, 3, 4, <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.1-2Chr.5.14">2Chr 5:1-14</reference> and 6. <div eID="gen32479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32480" type="x-p"/> As the prophet knew that the Chaldeans had utterly destroyed the temple, he thought it necessary to preserve an exact description of it, that on their restoration the people might build one on the same model. As to allegorical meanings relative to this temple, I can say nothing: God has given no data by which any thing of this kind can be known or applied; and as to those who have labored in this way, perhaps "Solomon's Temple Spiritualized, by John Bunyan," is equally good with their well-intended inventions. Those who wish to enter much into the particulars of this temple must have recourse to the more voluminous expositors, who on this subject seem to have thought that they could never say enough. See also the accompanying map.
entries.90e571d5a00e9221a8dd6a94a7344e72aef57e46: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32481" type="x-p"/> Set me upon a very high mountain - Mount Moriah, the mount on which Solomon's temple was built, <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.1">2Chr 3:1</reference>.
entries.5c0b296f254b00ab51ceb3ab473e453d1c665ada: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen32481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32482" type="x-p"/> A man, whose appearance was like - brass - Like bright polished brass, which strongly reflected the rays of light. Probably he had what we would term a nimbus or glory round his head. This was either an angel; or, as some think, a personal appearance of our blessed Lord.
entries.70e88acec11cecb2c8c5a05a0178f1c7e375091f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen32482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32483" type="x-p"/> Declare all that thou seest to the house of Israel - That they may know how to build the second temple, when they shall be restored from their captivity.
entries.0b386c62941137e26b43be69e4ccafbeb1cfa2cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32484" type="x-p"/> A measuring reed of six cubits long - The Hebrew cubit is supposed to be about twenty and a half inches; and a palm, about three inches more; the length of the rod about ten feet six inches. <div eID="gen32484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32485" type="x-p"/> The breadth - one reed; and the height, one reed - As this wall was as broad as it was high, it must have been a kind of parapet, which was carried, of the same dimensions, all round the temple. See AAAA in the plan.
entries.8ee8f16016cb1f7fe383f3ad6e77c914cb005a32: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen32485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32486" type="x-p"/> Went up the stairs thereof - As the temple was built upon an eminence, there must have been steps on the outside, opposite to each door, to ascend by. And it appears there were steps to go up from one court to another, see <reference osisRef="Eze.40.22">Eze 40:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.26">Eze 40:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.34">Eze 40:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.37">Eze 40:37</reference>; and also from the court of the priests to the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.49">Eze 40:49</reference>. See MMMMM in the plan.
entries.e57fb8c97c682b4e3b84bcde0fff3b81e4a479c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32487" type="x-p"/> And every little chamber was one reed - These were the chambers of the buildings which were within the inclosure of the temple round the court, and these chambers appear to have been numerous. See the map, which has been carefully copied from that of Calmet.
entries.837c8a7ec9fd83dc848acedbb24b7356aa320fd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32488" type="x-p"/> The porch of the gate - See account of the gates in the plan.
entries.da40846e0f35da6111c4a153ad88181fc8243b2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32489" type="x-p"/> Fifty cubits - The length of the building. See MMMMM in the plan.
entries.25ca9bd3852948238262b71b3ebe6a14f2dd09b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32490" type="x-p"/> The outward court - This was the court of the people.
entries.0cd6a0b25f721b2209617f56487b0dd62050ab46: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen32490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32491" type="x-p"/> And the little chambers thereof were three, etc. - See the plan. <div eID="gen32491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32492" type="x-p"/> Arches - Porch. The arch was not known at this period.
entries.7c71cf7f5448da5b51534a7bc8a948cdfab513c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen32492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32493" type="x-p"/> According to these measures - The same measures that had been used at the eastern court.
entries.579d7e58b5171e26f4279114ccef37f9b1561523: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen32493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32494" type="x-p"/> And the arches round about were five and twenty cubits long - That the five cubits broad should be read twenty-five is evident from <reference osisRef="Eze.40.21">Eze 40:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.25">Eze 40:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.29">Eze 40:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.33">Eze 40:33</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eze.40.36">Eze 40:36</reference>, The word ועשרים veesrim, twenty, has probably been lost out of the text. Indeed the whole verse is wanting in two of Kennicott's MSS., one of De Rossi's, and one of mine, (Cod. B.) It has been added in the margin of mine by a later hand. It is reported to have been anciently wanting in many MSS.
entries.3f4ee962dbc660cc8af91257cd900491dc5c96a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen32494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32495" type="x-p"/> The porch of the gate - The north gate of the court of the priests. See Q in the plan. <div eID="gen32495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32496" type="x-p"/> Two tables - Some say of marble. See dddd in the plan.
entries.36bdd7aa60e4957324497d423515ea688ddad72c: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen32496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32497" type="x-p"/> Four tables - These were in the porch of the north gate, in the court of the priests: on them they slew, flayed, and cut up the victims. See dddd in the plan.
entries.cd3f676e80ff38b1b390515dce7be912c512a828: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen32497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32498" type="x-p"/> He measured the court - This was the court of the priests. See FFF in the plan.
entries.ebcf4b81375f07db01c3c0260e4e73d78ad584c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen32498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32499" type="x-p"/> Breadth of the gate - It is evident that the gate was a bivalve, or had folding doors. The length of the porch was twenty cubits. Josephus says the vestibule was twenty cubits long and ten broad. Antiq. lib. 8:3, 2.
entries.b1f4c24002017f6306470919ea55901f2a2acf75: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen32499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32500" type="x-p"/> By the steps - This was a flight of steps that led to the temple; there were eight steps in each flight. See YY in the plan.  <chapter eID="Ezek.40"/> <div eID="gen32500" type="x-p"/>

entries.db7a257b9cd54b9ebf85d55b65d58f2d44e544b8: <div eID="gen15206" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Review of Ezekiel 40-48</title> <div sID="gen15207" type="x-p"/> Having now completed our exposition in detail, if we take a survey of the substance of the entire vision in Ezekiel 40-48, on comparing it with the preceding prophecies of the restoration of Israel (Ezekiel 34-37), we obtain the following picture of the new constitution of the kingdom of God: - When the Lord shall gather the sons of Israel from their banishment among the heathen, and bring them back to Canaan, so that they shall dwell therein as a united people under the rule of His servant David, then shall they, on the fresh distribution of the land according to the full extent to which God promised it to the patriarchs, and indicated the boundaries thereof through Moses (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.15-Ezek.47.20">Eze 47:15-20</reference>), set apart the central portion of it as a heave for the sanctuary and His servants, the priests and Levites, as well as for the capital and its labourers, and also give to the prince a possession of his own on both sides of this heave. In the central point of the heave, which occupies a square space of twenty-five thousand rods in length and breadth, the temple is to stand upon a high mountain, and cover, with its courts, a space of five hundred cubits square; and round about it a space of five hundred rods on every side is to form a boundary between the holy and the common. The glory of Jehovah will enter into the temple and dwell therein for ever; and the temple, in its whole extent, will be most holy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1-Ezek.43.12">Eze 43:1-12</reference>). Round about this the priests receive a tract of land of twenty-five thousand rods in length and ten thousand in breadth to dwell in as a sanctuary for the sanctuary; and by their side, toward the north, the Levites receive an area of similar size for dwelling-places; but toward the south, a tract of land of twenty-five thousand rods in length and five thousand rods in breadth is to be the property of the city; and in the centre of this area, the city, with its open space, is to cover a square of five thousand rods in length and breadth; and the rest of the land on both sides is to be given to the labourers of the city out of all Israel for their maintenance.
